{{Short description|Statement in probability theory}}
{{redirect|Dynkin's lemma|the statement about <math>\lambda</math>-systems|Dynkin system#Sierpiński–Dynkin's π-λ theorem}}
In [[probability theory]], the '''Doob–Dynkin lemma''', named after [[Joseph L. Doob]] and [[Eugene Dynkin]] (also known as the '''factorization lemma'''), characterizes the situation when one [[random variable]] is a function of another by the [[subset|inclusion]] of the [[sigma algebra|<math>\sigma</math>-algebras]] generated by the random variables. The usual statement of the lemma is formulated in terms of one random variable being [[measurable function|measurable]] with respect to the <math>\sigma</math>-algebra generated by the other.

The lemma plays an important role in the [[conditional expectation]] in probability theory, where it allows replacement of the conditioning on a [[random variable]] by conditioning on the [[sigma-algebra|<math>\sigma</math>-algebra]] that is [[Sigma algebra#.CF.83-algebra generated by a function|generated]] by the random variable.

==Notations and introductory remarks==
In the lemma below, <math>\mathcal{B}[0,1]</math> is the <math>\sigma</math>-algebra of [[Borel set]]s on <math> [0,1]. </math> If <math>T\colon X\to Y,</math> and <math>(Y,{\mathcal Y})</math> is a measurable space, then
:<math>\sigma(T)\ \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\ \{T^{-1}(S)\mid S\in {\mathcal Y}\} </math>
is the smallest <math>\sigma</math>-algebra on <math>X</math> such that <math>T</math> is <math> \sigma(T) / {\mathcal Y} </math>-measurable. 

==Statement of the lemma==
Let <math>T\colon \Omega\rightarrow\Omega'</math> be a function, and <math>(\Omega',\mathcal{A}') </math> a measurable space. A function <math>f\colon \Omega\rightarrow [0,1] </math> is <math> \sigma(T) / \mathcal{B}[0,1] </math>-measurable if and only if <math>f=g\circ T,</math> for some <math> \mathcal{A}' / \mathcal{B}[0,1] </math>-measurable <math>g\colon \Omega' \to [0,1]. </math><ref>{{Cite book| last=Kallenberg| first=Olav| title=Foundations of Modern Probability| year=1997| page=7| publisher=Springer| isbn=0-387-94957-7 |author-link=Olav Kallenberg }}</ref>

'''Remark.''' The "if" part simply states that the composition of two measurable functions is measurable. The "only if" part is proven below.

{| role="presentation" class="wikitable mw-collapsible mw-collapsed"
| '''Proof.'''
|-
|
Let <math>f</math> be <math>\sigma(T) / \mathcal{B}[0,1]</math>-measurable.

First, note that, by the above descriptive definition of <math>\sigma(T)</math> as the set of preimages of <math>\mathcal{A}'</math>-measurable sets under <math>T</math>, we know that if <math>A \in \sigma(T)</math>, then there exists some <math>A' \in \mathcal{A}'</math> such that <math>A = T^{-1}(A')</math>.

Now, assume that <math>f = \mathbf{1}_A</math> is an [[indicator function|indicator]] of some set <math>A \in \sigma(T)</math>. If we identify <math>A' \in \mathcal{A}'</math> such that <math>A = T^{-1}(A')</math>, then the function <math>g = \mathbf{1}_{A'}</math> suits the requirement, and since <math>A \in \sigma(T)</math>, such a set <math>A' \in \mathcal{A}'</math> always exists. By linearity, the claim extends to any [[simple function|simple measurable function]] <math>f.</math>

Let <math> f </math> be [[measurable function|measurable]] but not necessarily simple. As explained in the article on [[simple function]]s, <math>f</math> is a pointwise limit of a monotonically non-decreasing sequence <math>f_n \geq 0</math> of simple functions. The previous step guarantees that <math>f_n = g_n \circ T, </math> for some measurable <math> g_n. </math> The supremum <math> \textstyle g(x)=\sup_{ n \geq 1} g_n(x) </math> exists on the entire <math> \Omega' </math> and is measurable. (The article on [[measurable function]]s explains why supremum of a sequence of measurable functions is measurable). For every <math>x \in \operatorname{Im}T,</math> the sequence <math>g_n(x)</math> is non-decreasing, so <math> \textstyle g|_{\operatorname{Im}T}(x) = \lim_{ n \to \infty} g_n|_{\operatorname{Im}T}(x) </math> which shows that <math> f = g \circ T. </math>
|}

'''Remark.''' The lemma remains valid if the space <math> ([0,1],\mathcal{B}[0,1]) </math> is replaced with <math> (S,\mathcal{B}(S)), </math> where <math> S \subseteq [-\infty,\infty], </math> <math> S </math> is bijective with <math> [0,1], </math> and the bijection is measurable in both directions.

By definition, the measurability of <math> f </math> means that <math>f^{-1}(S)\in \sigma(T)</math> for every Borel set <math>S \subseteq [0,1].</math> Therefore <math>\sigma(f) \subseteq \sigma(T),</math> and the lemma may be restated as follows.

'''Lemma.''' Let <math>T\colon \Omega\rightarrow\Omega', </math> <math>f\colon \Omega\rightarrow [0,1], </math>  and <math>(\Omega',\mathcal{A}') </math> is a measurable space. Then <math> f = g\circ T, </math> for some <math> \mathcal{A}' / \mathcal{B}[0,1] </math>-measurable <math>g\colon \Omega' \to [0,1], </math> if and only if <math>\sigma(f) \subseteq \sigma(T)</math>.
